h1:
Pang Sida Trip
Butterfly Season, Early Rains
intro: From June through late July, Pang Sida National Park turns into a different place altogether. The first rains of the year leave the forest a fresh green, the waterfalls run full, and hundreds of butterfly species gather at the salt licks along the streams — enough that locals call it the "butterfly city of the eastern forest." This is an hour-by-hour 2-day, 1-night plan: watch butterflies in the late morning, swim at the falls in the afternoon, then camp and fall asleep to the sound of the forest. Written from park info and reviews by people who've actually been.

blocks.html: Pang Sida is a large park spanning Sa Kaeo into Prachinburi, part of the Dong Phaya Yen–Khao Yai World Heritage forest complex. From Sa Kaeo town you drive north on Highway 3462 for about 27 kilometers to reach the headquarters — closer to Bangkok than you'd think. It's roughly a 3.5- to 4-hour drive from Bangkok, which makes it a good weekend trip if you want to escape into real forest without going far.

The heart of this trip is timing. The butterflies only come out in big numbers in the early rainy season, and they only come down to drink at the salt licks during the sunny late morning. The waterfalls are at their best in this same window too, since the water has just arrived. So the plan is to watch butterflies from morning until noon, then head to the falls in the afternoon.

Pang Sida's butterflies are out in the greatest numbers from mid-June to late July, because it's the start of the rainy season — the soil is damp, plants put out fresh shoots, and the caterpillars grow up and emerge as butterflies all at once in a big generation. That's why the park holds its annual butterfly-watching season then. Pang Sida has more than 500 recorded butterfly species, from swallowtails and birdwings to the tiny ones that come down to drink water in swarms.

items: Peak window — late June to mid-July; if the rains come on time, the butterflies are at their most abundant
Best time to watch — around 9am–noon, when the sun comes out after a night of rain and the butterflies gather at the salt licks
The trade-off — it's the rainy season, some paths are slippery, and certain falls may close if the water surges; go in knowing nature is out of anyone's control

blocks.title: Check before you set off
blocks.html: The butterflies don't come out the same amount every day — it depends on the previous night's rain and the sun. Call the park ahead at 081-862-1511 or 037-247-948 to ask about that day's conditions, so you don't end up disappointed.

items: Entry (Thai nationals) — adults 40 THB, children 20 THB · foreigners adults 200, children 100 THB
Vehicle fee — charged per car at the park's rate (a sedan is a few tens of baht)
Opening hours — daily 8:30am–4:30pm, but if you're camping overnight you can stay on
Getting there — from Sa Kaeo town take Highway 3462 north for 27 km; the park is on the right and well signed
Transport — you really need your own vehicle; there's no public transport inside the park and the distances between spots are too far to walk

blocks.html: This plan is built for self-drivers. You arrive at the park in the late morning of day one, in time for the midday butterflies, swim at the falls in the afternoon, then camp overnight. On day two you wake up early for the spots that take a longer walk, before heading home.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Butterflies at the salt lick + Pang Sida Waterfall

items.note: Take the motorway and Route 33 toward Sa Kaeo, stopping for breakfast on the way; allow extra time for traffic getting out of the city

items.activity: Arrive at Pang Sida park headquarters
items.note: Pay the entry fee, use the restroom, top up on water, and ask the rangers which salt lick has the most butterflies today

The salt lick beside the stream near the headquarters is where butterflies come down to drink in swarms. Wear light or bright colors, and skip perfume and insect repellent — the scent drives the butterflies away
There's a simple park restaurant, or you can pack your own lunch. The butterflies start thinning out after midday, which lines up nicely with the meal

About 800 meters from the headquarters and an easy walk; roughly 10 meters tall with a pool you can swim in along parts of it. The water runs strong in the rainy season, so stick to the shallow pool and watch for slippery rocks

items.activity: Heart of Dong Phaya Yen nature trail
items.note: A short walking loop around the headquarters to take in the forest and the plant life; some days you'll spot more butterflies along the way

items.activity: Check into the campground and set up
items.note: The Pang Sida campground is close to the headquarters, the falls, and the butterfly salt lick. Cook, sit back, and listen to the forest; on a clear night you'll see plenty of stars

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Pha Takhian Waterfall + grasslands before heading home

items.activity: Wake to morning in the forest
items.note: Rainy-season mornings often have a thin mist and pleasantly cool air; brew some coffee and shoot the early light
About 3 km from the headquarters, with a bit more walking to get in. It's taller than Pang Sida and flows in beautiful tiers in the rainy season. The trail is genuine forest, so wear non-slip shoes

items.activity: Pack up camp, stop at the viewpoint and grasslands
items.note: Pang Sida has open grasslands and viewpoints; get your mountain-view photos before leaving the park
Drive down to eat in town, where there are plenty of Isan and local restaurants. Refuel before the drive back
If you have time to spare, stop at a souvenir market or another sight in Sa Kaeo town before heading into Bangkok

blocks.text: Which waterfalls to visit in Pang Sida

items.name: Pang Sida Waterfall
items.blurb: The closest to the headquarters, about 800 meters' walk from the parking lot. Roughly 10 meters tall with a pool to swim in — good for families and anyone who'd rather not walk far.

items.name: Pha Takhian Waterfall
items.blurb: About 3 km from the headquarters with a forest hike to reach it. Taller, with lovely tiered flows in the rainy season — good for those who enjoy walking.

items.name: Khwae Makha Waterfall
items.blurb: Deep in the forest, with a long, demanding walk. Best for adventurers after a quiet, crowd-free waterfall — you should have a ranger to guide you.

items.name: Huai Nam Yen
items.blurb: A ranger station 20 km from the headquarters, home to wild Siamese crocodiles and with another campground. Remote in feel.

blocks.text: Lodging, camping, and what to pack

blocks.html: Pang Sida has both park bungalows and campgrounds. Book ahead through the Department of National Parks website at nps.dnp.go.th. The butterfly season is busy, so reserve several days in advance. There are two campgrounds: the Pang Sida ground (near the headquarters, the falls, and the butterfly salt lick) and the Huai Nam Yen ground, which is farther out and quieter. Tents and bedding are available to rent if you'd rather not haul your own.

items: Clothing — light or bright colors help butterflies come closer; avoid all black · bring a rain jacket and something warm for the night you camp
Footwear — non-slip or hiking shoes, since the rainy-season trails are slippery and muddy
Repellent — you'll definitely want some, but it scares off butterflies while you're watching them, so apply it only in the evening and at night
Water & food — bring some of your own drinking water and snacks; the park shops are limited and close early
Cash — there's no phone signal at some spots, so carry cash for the entry fee and equipment rental

blocks.text: How to see the most butterflies

items: Go between 9am and noon, when the sun is out after the rain and the butterflies gather at the salt lick to drink in swarms
Stay still and don't chase them — butterflies spook easily; sit quietly for a while and they'll come to you
Skip perfume, sprays, and strong-smelling creams; chemical scents make butterflies flee
Bring a zoom lens or a good phone camera — butterflies are small and hard to shoot up close
Respect nature: don't collect, don't catch, don't litter — Pang Sida is a conservation area

blocks.title: Make peace with the rain
blocks.html: This is a genuine rainy-season trip — some days it can rain all day, the butterflies won't come out, and the falls may be too murky and forceful to swim in. Plan a backup indoor activity, or accept that you'll get the rainforest atmosphere instead — it's still worth it.

blocks.text: Extend your trip around Sa Kaeo

blocks.html: If you have more than two days, Pang Sida pairs easily with other sights in Sa Kaeo. On the way back, stop at Khao Chakan, a limestone mountain rising out of the fields, or carry on toward Aranyaprathet for street food and a wander through Rong Kluea Market. History buffs into the Khmer past can add Sdok Kok Thom temple — enough to round out a tidy 3-day trip.

faq.q: When is the best time to see butterflies at Pang Sida?
faq.a: The early rainy season, roughly mid-June to late July, is when the butterflies are out in the greatest numbers, and the best time to see lots of them is 9am–noon — after a night of rain followed by sun, when they come down to drink at the salt licks beside the streams in swarms. It varies day to day, so it's worth calling the park first at 081-862-1511.

faq.q: How much is entry to Pang Sida National Park and what are the hours?
faq.a: Thai nationals pay 40 THB for adults and 20 THB for children; foreigners pay 200 THB for adults and 100 THB for children, plus a per-vehicle fee. It's open daily 8:30am–4:30pm, and you can stay on if you're camping overnight.

faq.q: Do you need your own car to visit Pang Sida, and how do you get there?
faq.a: You really should have your own vehicle, since there's no public transport inside the park and the spots are far apart. From Sa Kaeo town take Highway 3462 north for 27 kilometers; the park is on the right. From Bangkok it's about a 3.5- to 4-hour drive.

faq.q: How do you book camping at Pang Sida, and is there gear to rent?
faq.a: Book through the Department of National Parks website at nps.dnp.go.th. There are two campgrounds — the Pang Sida ground near the headquarters and the Huai Nam Yen ground, which is farther out — and tents and bedding are available to rent. The butterfly season is busy, so reserve several days ahead.

faq.q: Can you swim at Pang Sida Waterfall in the rainy season, and is it dangerous?
faq.a: Pang Sida Waterfall, near the headquarters, has a pool you can swim in along parts of it, but in the rainy season the water runs strong and the rocks are slippery, so stick to the shallow pool and be careful. If it rains hard or the water surges it may close temporarily — always check with the rangers on site before getting in.
